content:
Hello. I am interested in combining Lean with graph visualization to represent the structure and progress of formal proofs. I am curious whether anyone here has been thinking about similar questions.

My particular interest is in modularizing a long proof into declarations and smaller obligations, while clearly distinguishing between parts that have been verified and parts that remain open or have failed verification. Representing these relationships as a dependency graph could make it easier to see what has already been established, what remains to be proved, and which unresolved obligations are blocking the final result. I believe such a graph could serve as a compass during long and complicated formalization projects.

I am currently developing this idea as an open-source project called ProofFrontier (https://github.com/jivaprime/prooffrontier). Rather than treating verification as only a pass-or-fail judgment, ProofFrontier aims to preserve unfinished proofs and open assumptions explicitly in the graph, so that the remaining research frontier stays visible.

In the longer term, I would like to make Lean verification results and their corresponding graph representations shareable among multiple contributors. The goal is to help people understand the current state of a proof project, identify meaningful tasks, and collaborate without losing sight of its dependencies and limitations.

Would anyone on Zulip be interested in this methodology or style of collaboration? I would also be grateful for pointers to related work, existing tools, or feedback on the project’s design.
